extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners/agents/attorneys preparing or prosecuting design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, filing, and examining U.S. design patent applications (content, drawings, claims, priority, and related procedural and substantive requirements). Intended to govern prosecution and examination practice for design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for design patents (35 U.S.C. 171)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whoever invents any new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions of the patent statute that relate to patents for inventions apply to design patents except as otherwise provided; design patent applications are not included in the PCT; see 37 CFR 1.151 and 1.152-1.155.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a design (claimed subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a design patent application, the subject matter which is claimed is the design embodied in or applied to an article of manufacture (or portion thereof) and not the article itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design consists of visual characteristics/appearance (configuration, surface ornamentation, or combination). Design is inseparable from the article, must be definite, preconceived, capable of reproduction, and not merely chance result of a method. The overall appearance creates the impression on an observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents protect appearance (vs. utility patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A 'utility patent' protects the way an article is used and works (35 U.S.C. 101), while a 'design patent' protects the way an article looks (35 U.S.C. 171)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An article may have both utility and ornamentality and may be eligible for both types of patents; utility/ornamentality often intertwine—examination must respect differing legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in term and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of design patent is 14 years from date of grant (35 U.S.C. 173); utility patent term (post-1995) is 20 years from filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No maintenance fees are required for design patents (unlike utility patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-claim requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications may include only a single claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim must be in formal terms to the ornamental design for the article (specifying name) as shown, or as shown and described (37 CFR 1.153). More than one claim is neither required nor permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction practice in design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction between plural, distinct inventions is mandatory in design patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application contains plural distinct designs, the examiner must require restriction (see MPEP § 1504.05).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority and provisional benefit limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) for design patents is 6 months (not 12). Design applications may not claim the benefit of a provisional application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants claiming priority must supply certified copies and may be required to provide translations; notation requirements on file wrappers must be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements and arrangement of a design application
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application has the elements required of a utility application (see Chapter 600) and should follow the arrangement in 37 CFR 1.154.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested order: transmittal forms, preamble (name, title, brief description of nature/intended use), cross-references, federally sponsored research statement, description of figures, feature description, single claim, drawings/photographs, executed oath/declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and preamble requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the design must designate the particular article (name generally known and used by the public) and the preamble should state applicant name, title of design, and brief description of nature/intended use (37 CFR 1.153, 1.154).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title must correspond to claim language; examiner should allow latitude but require amendment only if title/claim are clearly misdescriptive, inaccurate, or unclear. Use of 'or the like' for environment is acceptable; using broad ambiguous titles that broaden the article is objectionable. Amendments to title require antecedent basis and must not introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: generally unnecessary but permissible statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any description beyond a brief reference to drawings is ordinarily not required but may be included; permissible statements include descriptions of unillustrated portions, purpose of broken lines, nature/environmental use, and a 'characteristic features' statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If figure descriptions are provided and are unclear/inaccurate the examiner should object and suggest clearer language. Characteristic features statement may be included but does not determine patentability; overall appearance controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible specification statements (new matter and improper subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers directed to solid-line parts, statements suggesting modifications not illustrated, and descriptions of unrelated function are not permitted in the specification of an issued design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements may be included in original application to provide antecedent basis for future amendment, but cannot broaden claimed design beyond drawings; including them in issued patent is improper and should be canceled or objected to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic feature statement caution
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'characteristic features' statement describing a particular feature of novelty or nonobviousness may be permissible but 'the patentability of the claimed design is not based on the specified feature but rather on a comparison of the overall appearance of the design with the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase such statements succinctly (e.g., 'The characteristic feature of the design resides in [...]'). Inclusion may later serve to limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are essential and must comply with 37 CFR 1.84 and 1.152
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must be represented by a drawing that contains a sufficient number of views to constitute a complete disclosure of the appearance of the design; appropriate surface shading should be used; broken lines may be used for visible environmental structure only; color drawings/photographs limited by petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any detail shown in drawings or photographs deposited with the original application constitutes an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design unless explicitly disclaimed in original papers. Inconsistencies among views should be objected to; severe inconsistencies can render the claim nonenabled under 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity for good drawings (enablement / sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim and must be so clear and complete that nothing regarding the design is left to conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient drawings may be fatal to validity under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, and may adversely affect effective filing dates for continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Views: required and when omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings should contain sufficient views to disclose the complete appearance (front, rear, top, bottom, sides); perspective views suggested; duplicative or flat views lacking ornamentality may be omitted if explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If left/right sides are identical, provide one side and a statement that the other side is identical/mirror image; sectional views solely showing internal construction are unnecessary and may cause confusion; sectional views only permitted to clarify exterior contour when necessary and must have antecedent basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate and adequate surface shading should be used to show the character or contour of surfaces; solid black surface shading is not permitted except to represent the color black or color contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblique line shading for transparent/translucent/highly polished surfaces; line shading and stippling can show contrasts in materials broadly without limiting to specific colors/materials; lack of required shading in filed drawing may render design nonenabling or constitute new matter if added later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines: environment and boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines commonly disclose environmental structure or define the bounds of the claim; broken lines form no part of the claimed design when used as environment and may be used to indicate boundaries that are not present in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken lines cannot be used to show hidden planes/surfaces, or to indicate lesser importance of a portion. If broken lines cross full-line design, specification must explicitly identify their purpose. Adding non-straight broken-line boundaries may introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must show claimed design in full (solid) lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornamental design being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing; dotted/broken lines cannot be used to indicate immaterial features of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no portions of a claimed design that are immaterial or unimportant; environmental structure may be in broken lines but claimed subject matter must be in full lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs and color drawings rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are normally required in black ink; photographs are acceptable only where ink drawings cannot illustrate the invention or photographs show ornamental effects more clearly; color photographs/drawings require petition (37 CFR 1.84(a)(2), 1.152(a)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs must comply with 37 CFR 1.84(b); photographs and ink drawings should not be combined; photographs deposited without required disclaimers may make the detail integral and require formal color drawings or black-and-white lined to represent color; poor quality photos lead to objections and possible rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 if details/shape are not clearly disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment disclosure and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface 'treatment' (indicia, contrasting color/materials, graphic representations, other ornamentation) must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment per se is not proper subject matter for a design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface treatment shown in drawings/photographs is prima facie integral to the claimed design. Removal of two-dimensional surface treatment or reducing it to broken lines may be permitted if underlying design is apparent; removal of three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration introduces new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of detail shown in informal drawings/photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any detail shown in informal drawings or photographs deposited with the original application papers constitutes an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design unless a specific disclaimer appears in the original application papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific disclaimer in the original application (specification or on drawings/photographs) provides antecedent basis for omission of disclaimed details in later-filed drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall-appearance test for novelty and nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the patentability of a design, it is the overall appearance of the claimed design which must be taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic feature statements do not substitute for overall appearance analysis; comparisons to prior art consider the total visual impression (see In re Rosen, In re Leslie).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112 considerations (enablement and claim definiteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim defines the subject matter which the applicant regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph); drawings must enable the claimed design (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear or inconsistent figure descriptions/drawings may be objected to or may lead to a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 as nonenabled; amendments introducing new drawing matter are prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and new matter prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to title, claim language, drawings, or specification must have antecedent basis in the original disclosure and may not introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132; MPEP guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding details, changing configuration/shape, or non-straight broken-line boundaries not present in original disclosure can constitute prohibited new matter and may cause rejection or loss of priority benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of earlier U.S. filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for patent which is disclosed in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112 in an earlier-filed application by the same inventor may have the same effect as though filed on the date of the prior application if filed before patenting/abandonment and contains or is amended to contain a specific reference to the earlier filed application (35 U.S.C. 120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CIPs that change shape/configuration generally do not get the benefit of the earlier filing date. If the earlier application is fatally defective under 112, later CIPs cannot rely on 120 for benefit. Indicate benefit statements in the first line of the specification when claiming benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 (foreign priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: No application for design patent shall be entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim therefor and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed before issue fee is paid or at a time during pendency as required by the Commissioner, but not earlier than six months after U.S. filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification shall show the date of the application and filing of specification; translations and other information may be required; failure to file required papers can forfeit priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part caution for design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Design case law holds that any change to the shape or configuration of a design disclosed in an earlier application constitutes an entirely new design that cannot rely upon the earlier one for priority (In re Salmon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later-filed application that changes shape/configuration does not satisfy written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, under 35 U.S.C. 120 and is not entitled to benefit of the earlier filing date; examiner should include warning paragraph in first action when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance and issue fee requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If, on examination, it appears applicant is entitled to a design patent, a notice of allowance will be sent calling for payment of the issue fee (§ 1.18(b)). If the issue fee is not paid within three months of the notice of allowance, the application shall be regarded as abandoned (37 CFR 1.155).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term of design patent is 14 years from date of grant (35 U.S.C. 173).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue, reexamination, protest references
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue practice (MPEP Ch. 1400) and reexamination practice (MPEP Ch. 2200) apply to design patents with specific design-related fee and term limits; protest procedures referenced to MPEP Ch. 1900.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term of a design patent may not be extended by reissue; follow respective chapters for practice and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent overlap with copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: An ornamental design may be copyrighted as a work of art and may also be subject matter of a design patent; author/inventor need not elect between copyright and design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of a copyright notice is permitted subject to size/location limits and required waiver language in the specification; waiver must include specific language permitting facsimile reproduction by anyone of the patent document as it appears in the PTO records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of copyright notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright notice must be adjacent to the copyrighted material; if on a drawing it must be 1/8 to 1/4 inch and placed within the sight of the drawing below the figure; content limited to elements required by law (e.g., '© 1983 John Doe').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A waiver statement (specified language) must be included in the specification, preferably as the first paragraph, allowing facsimile reproduction as in PTO records; inclusion after Notice of Allowance requires meeting 37 CFR 1.312 criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent overlap with trademark and trademark use limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent and trademark may be obtained on same subject matter; use of trademarks in design patent specifications is permitted under limited circumstances; trademarks alone or coupled with 'type' should not be used in the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must object to trademarks used in the title; if trademark appears in drawing, the specification must include a statement preceding the claim identifying the trademark material forming part of the claimed design and the name of the owner. Derogatory use of a trademark will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 as offensive subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive subject matter prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Derogatory or offensive subject matter in a design application is improper subject matter for design patent protection and will be rejected (e.g., derogatory use of trademarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases (Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders v. Pussycat Cinema; Coca-Cola Co. v. Gemini Rising) as authority for rejection when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal description of broken lines required
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific statement must be used to describe broken lines used as environment: '-- The broken line showing of [1] is for illustrative purposes only and forms no part of the claimed design. --' and for boundaries: '-- The broken line(s) which define the bounds of the claimed design form no part thereof. --'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert the appropriate statement in the specification preceding the claim when broken lines are present; ensure brackets replaced with the correct structure names and wording ('must be'/'has been').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of informal drawings/photographs and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: When informal color drawings or photographs are deposited with original application without the required disclaimer, formal color drawings/photographs or black-and-white drawings lined to represent color will be required; when detail in informal drawings does not constitute an integral part of the design, an original specific disclaimer must appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting of petitions to accept color photographs/drawings may be conditioned on submission of required materials and fees; subsequently the examiner may object to quality and require corrected submissions before issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken line boundaries added post-filing limited to straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no boundary line is shown in a design application as originally filed, but the specification makes clear the boundary is a straight broken line connecting the ends of existing full lines, applicant may amend to add straight broken line connecting the ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any broken line boundary other than a straight broken line may constitute new matter prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(a)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of surface shading vs. lining for color (clarity caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the formal drawing in an application is 'lined for color', a statement 'The drawing is lined for color.' should be inserted in the specification to avoid confusion that the lining may be surface treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lining for color may interfere with clear showing required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, because surface shading cannot be used to define the contours of the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies among views must be corrected
rubrics_metrics.description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object to the drawings and request that the views be made consistent; inconsistencies that make overall appearance unclear may lead to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, as nonenabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections should be raised and applicant given opportunity to correct; provide reasons/citation in examiner's objection paragraphs.
